video_title: The Inference Frontier: 10x Faster Models to Self-Optimizing AI — Philip Kiely & Ali Taha, Baseten
gist: Baseten's Philip Kiely and Ali Taha walk through the full economics and engineering of modern LLM inference: cache-aware routing, prefill/decode disaggregation, speculators, and NVFP4 quantization stack to roughly 4-10x speedups over an off-the-shelf engine, and they argue quantizing MORE layers can raise fidelity when errors cancel. They are bearish on mega-kernels and on standalone AI ASICs (Nvidia's GPUs are already becoming ASIC-like), bullish on KV-cache infrastructure as the Rubin-era bottleneck, and describe GLM 5.2 already writing the GPU kernels inside their own inference engine.

insights.claim: Baseten routes long requests with cache-aware routing that picks the replica with both free prefill workers and existing cached input, so a 200,000-token coding or agent request can skip most of prefill entirely.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Cache hit rate is a first-order cost driver for agentic workloads; providers without cache-aware routing will be structurally more expensive per token on long-context traffic.
insights.quote: So, the first thing that we're going to look at is some kind of cache aware routing

insights.claim: Baseten has disaggregated prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools on certain models, with one set producing the KV cache and first token and a second set running iterative decode.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: PD disaggregation requires enough hardware and traffic to be worth it, which favors scaled inference providers over small self-hosters.

insights.claim: A speculator is a small parasite layer that predicts roughly three tokens ahead which the full model then verifies in one forward pass, accepting or rejecting them, and a domain-specific draft model can be trained to hit near-100% acceptance on that domain.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Custom speculators are a defensible per-customer moat that only dedicated deployments can capture, not shared APIs.

insights.claim: Speculators for a large model are roughly one billion parameters or about 1/60 of the original model, sometimes a single layer, and must run on the same hardware as the target model, creating orchestration and resource contention.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha and Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Speculation is not free capacity; the draft model eats GPU resources, which caps how far recursive speculation stacks can go.

insights.claim: Structured output is solved at inference time by compiling a state machine that constrains decoding to a format, which fixes malformed tool-call JSON but does nothing about the model calling the wrong tool or no tool.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Agent reliability failures attributed to 'bad JSON' are already solved; remaining tool-call failures are training and selection problems, not parsing problems.

insights.claim: The dominant tool-calling failure mode is a model that fails to close a request properly, never sees the tool result, and then hallucinates the result during decode — not sandbox escape or security containment.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Agent-eval budgets should target output-termination and post-training quality rather than sandbox isolation infrastructure.

insights.claim: Customers pushing millions of tokens per hour are materially cheaper paying per GPU-hour for a dedicated box than per token, shifting saturation risk onto the customer.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Per-token API revenue is a top-of-funnel product; the durable high-volume revenue is capacity rental, which has different gross-margin dynamics.
insights.quote: And more often than not it's like way cheaper if you're pushing like millions of tokens per hour if you just pay per hour instead of pay per token.

insights.claim: The observed customer journey is to try open models on pay-per-token APIs and then migrate the sticky use case to dedicated deployments, which Baseten says is rising demand for both tiers.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Serverless open-model APIs function as a conversion funnel; watch attach rates from shared to dedicated as the real growth metric for inference providers.

insights.claim: Reasons to move to a dedicated endpoint include a customer-specific speculative decoder, custom batch size and parallelism strategy, higher precision than NVFP4 if a quant fails your benchmarks, and avoiding noisy neighbors running 100 million tokens of benchmarking traffic.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: A concrete checklist for when enterprises should stop buying shared tokens; noisy-neighbor latency variance is an underrated migration trigger.

insights.claim: Baseten runs zero data retention on its model APIs, so it trains general speculators on public datasets chosen to mimic known-popular coding and agentic traffic rather than on actual customer prompts.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: ZDR is a sales asset but caps speculator quality on shared endpoints, structurally advantaging dedicated deployments where customer data can be used.

themes.theme: Day-zero model support is real engineering

insights.claim: Getting a token out of a newly released open model is easy because vLLM and SGLang maintainers often receive weights ahead of time and labs merge support PRs, but a production-ready API on a proprietary stack is substantially harder.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Day-one 'we support model X' announcements are near-meaningless as a differentiator; latency and fidelity a week later are the real signal.

insights.claim: Every new model release forces redoing quantization to NVFP4 for Blackwell, recalibrating it against intelligence regressions, and retraining a speculator using hidden states extracted from the real base model weights.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Speculator training requires the actual weights, so open-weight releases are a hard prerequisite for the fast-inference ecosystem — closed models cannot be optimized by third parties this way.

insights.claim: A Baseten engineer grafted Kimi's vision encoder onto GLM 5.2 by freezing both encoder and model weights and training only the projector, which is a handful of millions of parameters, reaching about 56% on MMLU without degrading text quality.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely and Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Modality retrofitting on open weights is cheap and non-destructive, meaning capability gaps in open models can be patched by third parties, not just labs.
insights.quote: And ultimately, what you get out of the system is all of a sudden you have Kimmy vision, GLM weights, and deep seek attention all in one model.

insights.claim: Inference providers actively swap inefficient layers out of new models — replacing MiniMax M3's full-attention layer with a GQA layer from another model — because full attention makes the KV cache non-sparse and O(N squared) costs explode.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Serving cost is now partly a function of the provider's willingness to surgically retrain layers, which widens the performance spread between providers on the same weights.

insights.claim: Support is not a day-zero event: after launch, real-world traffic surfaces bugs like GLM mode collapse where the model emitted the same token repeatedly at various temperatures, requiring weeks of ongoing patching for popular models.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: First-week reliability, not launch-day support, is what differentiates providers; buyers should stage traffic rather than cut over at launch.

insights.claim: Token-repetition collapse is an inference software problem, not a weights problem: identical weights on a different engine do not reproduce it, and it can be traced to kernel race conditions exposed only on clusters with slower node-to-node KV cache interconnects.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Model-quality complaints can be cluster-topology artifacts; blaming the lab or the quant is often wrong, and provider cluster heterogeneity is a hidden quality variable.
insights.quote: the same exact weights used with a different inference engine does not repeat the the problem

insights.claim: Most inference optimizations including KV caching and speculation are lossless; quantization is the one materially lossy optimization, governed by data format, which layers you quantize, and calibration to preserve outliers.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: When evaluating a provider's quality claims, quantization policy is the only place fidelity can actually be lost — interrogate that, not the routing stack.

insights.claim: Baseten defines inference quality as fidelity to a golden implementation of the model, with an internal standard that a customer should not be able to tell their API from the model author's official API.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Gives a testable purchasing criterion: run the lab's own reference API against the reseller on identical prompts.

insights.claim: Model labs now police provider quality directly — Kimi's vendor verifier called out providers including Amazon for degraded serving three to five months ago — because bad third-party serving gets blamed on the model, not the host.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely and Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Vendor-verifier scores are becoming a public quality benchmark that can damage a cloud provider's inference reputation; watch for more labs launching them.

insights.claim: Baseten research by intern Joshua showed quantizing MORE layers can raise fidelity because quantization errors from different layers cancel out, and which layers cancel can be predicted mathematically.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the industry heuristic that more quantization always means more loss — a genuine technical edge in cost-per-token if it generalizes.
insights.quote: you can predict which layers are going to have quantization errors that will cancel out with each other and you choose to quantize those layers

insights.claim: Baseten claims a 20% more heavily quantized GLM 5.2 than Nvidia's, yielding roughly 20% more throughput while measuring BETTER fidelity, proven via KL divergence between quantized and full-precision logit distributions rather than benchmark scores.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: KL divergence on logits is the more honest fidelity metric than eval scores; expect it to become the industry standard for quant claims.
insights.quote: So, instead of just scoring on the benchmarks, we scored the KL divergences between the logit distribution of the quantized model and the logit distribution of the original full precision model.

themes.theme: How much speed is actually on the table

insights.claim: A one-trillion-parameter model on a standard unoptimized API runs roughly 30 to 50 tokens per second per user, and Baseten targets 10x that, with 300 to 400 tokens per second achievable using best hardware, tuned speculator, full quantization, high cache hit rate and small latency-tuned batch size.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Quantifies the achievable spread between worst and best providers on identical open weights — a direct arbitrage for buyers on OpenRouter or Artificial Analysis.

insights.claim: The realistic provider-to-provider spread on the same model is more often 4x to 6x than the aggressive 10x, and normalizing for identical hardware and GPU count it narrows to roughly 2x to 4x from software optimizations alone.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely and Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Separates 'better engineering' from 'better hardware' when comparing inference vendors — much of a headline speed win is just newer GPUs.

insights.claim: The speedup stack decomposes as roughly 30-40% from BF16 to FP8 and another 30-40% from FP8 to NVFP4 (together roughly 2x), roughly 2x from a speculator, roughly 2x from disaggregation given enough hardware and traffic, plus double-digit percent from a better runtime.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: A quantified build-vs-buy model: each layer is hours-to-days of expert work but disaggregation has a steep first-time cost.
insights.quote: Speculator, roughly a 2x. Disag on top of that if you are able to get enough hardware and and put enough traffic through it, another roughly a 2x.

insights.claim: A normal operator renting a node of B200s no longer needs to quantize or train speculators themselves — open-source NVFP4 checkpoints exist, Nvidia ships one if nobody else does, and models like Kimi and GLM 5.2 ship their own multi-token-prediction heads.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: The commoditization of quantized checkpoints and speculators compresses the moat of mid-tier inference providers toward routing and infrastructure.

insights.claim: Inference remains an immature optimization domain where wins are measured in 20%, 100% and 200%, unlike quantitative finance where 5 basis points is news — and the field will only be solved when providers publish 1% improvements.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: A durable heuristic for how much alpha remains in inference optimization; the shrinking size of published gains is the maturity signal to watch.
insights.quote: When we publish optimizations, it's it's 20%, it's 100%, it's 200%.

insights.claim: Nvidia's Dynamo is a developer toolkit for moving KV cache around a cluster via NIXL rather than an out-of-box system, so pip installing it yields no automatic speedup and it is not yet a credible industry baseline.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Deflates expectations that Nvidia's open-source stack commoditizes inference providers; the integration work remains the value.
insights.quote: I would think of Dynamo as less of a sort of out-of-box system and more of a toolkit for building with.

themes.theme: Hardware trajectory: Blackwell, Rubin and the ASIC debate

insights.claim: Tensor parallelism shards the model across all GPUs and needs all-gather/all-reduce over a high-bandwidth interconnect like NVLink, while expert parallelism places whole experts on separate GPUs with a replicated small router and far less communication, so production systems combine both.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Explains why interconnect quality, not raw FLOPs, determines achievable latency — the core reason Rubin-era networking matters.
insights.quote: Tensor parallelism is not a good fit for local AI because it assumes a very high bandwidth interconnect like NVLink.

insights.claim: Latest-generation GPU memory sets a hard model-size ceiling: H100s carry 80GB each, B-series 180GB, and GB300s 288GB, so a 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi at NVFP4 needs about 1.4 terabytes and only fits across eight GB300s with room left for KV cache.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Frontier open-model releases are gated by top-end GPU memory availability, tying open-model adoption directly to GB300 supply.

insights.claim: Model sizes are set by what the latest inference hardware can serve — DeepSeek's 671-billion-parameter release pushed rapid Blackwell adoption — and labs increasingly match native quantization to target hardware, as with Nvidia Nemotron models shipping in NVFP4.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Model architecture releases are a leading indicator of GPU generation demand and vice versa; watch parameter counts as a proxy for hardware refresh pressure.

insights.claim: Mega-kernels are a dead-end optimization: fused kernels cannot avoid cross-GPU communication because of non-linearities like softmax, they are extremely hard to write well, and companies building them often do not run them in production because TensorRT-LLM and Modular kernels are faster.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: An explicitly contrarian bet against a hyped Silicon Valley research direction; relevant to anyone valuing kernel-fusion startups.
insights.quote: even the companies that have have worked at or people that I've spoken to who work at companies that do fused mega-kernels, they very very often don't end up running those in production

insights.claim: Rubin shifts inference engineering from a CUDA-kernel problem to a traditional hardware-infrastructure problem, with KV cache offloading, KV-aware routing and disaggregation becoming substantially more important given greater emphasis on CPU-GPU and GPU-GPU interconnect.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Predicts where inference value accrues next: cluster-level data movement software, which is exactly what Dynamo is designed for.
insights.quote: I think that themes around like KV cache offloading, KV aware routing, and and disaggregation are going to be substantially more important in the Rubin era

insights.claim: GPUs are trending toward being ASICs — tensor cores, TMAs, tensor memory and MMA instructions shaped around today's model head dimensions — so kernel writing matters less and orchestration matters more.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: If true, the skill premium shifts from CUDA engineers to infrastructure engineers, and Nvidia captures ASIC-like efficiency without giving up generality.

insights.claim: Standalone AI ASIC companies are hard to be bullish on because Nvidia is converging on ASIC-like specialization each generation, while burning weights into silicon is impractical when you want to fine-tune, quantize and ship new checkpoints monthly.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: A bearish frame on the AI-ASIC startup category from an operator who serves models daily; the counterargument is model longevity, not chip capability.
insights.quote: Burning weights into the chip is like impractical cuz you want to fine-tune, you want to optimize, you want to you want to quantize, you want to release new checkpoints of the model.

insights.claim: Video diffusion inference is structurally unlike LLM serving: no batching, each request lands on one GPU with no sharding, and the models are far smaller — Wan 2.2 is about 20 billion parameters, orders of magnitude below frontier LLMs.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Video inference economics are per-GPU-per-request, so capacity planning and unit economics do not transfer from LLM serving.

insights.claim: The open-versus-closed gap has essentially closed for LLMs but remains night-and-day for video, where open Wan 2.2 output is far behind Kling and Veo, and labs are closing their newer checkpoints (Wan 2.7 is not open source).
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Open-weight substitution risk is real for text APIs but not yet for video, protecting closed video-model pricing power.
insights.quote: If you look at the best video that you can generate today with an open-source model like 1.2.2 versus something like with Kling or Veo, the difference is night and day.

insights.claim: Media companies will pay 100x more for closed video models — $1,000 versus an optimized $10 — because quality dominates cost at that price point, creating a chicken-and-egg loop where low demand for open video models suppresses innovation and open checkpoint releases.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Cost optimization is not a wedge into media video workflows; open video model providers face a demand-side, not a price-side, problem.
insights.quote: So the it's like a chicken and egg cycle where less demand causes less innovation in the field which causes, you know, less open-source checkpoints to be released.

insights.claim: Video attention cost explodes quadratically: five seconds of 480p at 16fps compresses to roughly 35,000 latent tokens, making a one-minute full-attention cutscene effectively impossible within reasonable compute time.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Quantifies why long-form generative video is compute-blocked, setting a hard bound on near-term Hollywood-scale AI video.

insights.claim: The two escape routes from quadratic video attention are sparse attention (attending only to the top ~12.5% of spatially and temporally local tokens, which visibly degrades quality) or auto-regressive video, and no good open-source auto-regressive video models exist today.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Names the specific research unlock — open auto-regressive video — that would reprice the generative video market.
insights.quote: Auto regressive video seems to me like that is the bet that the future is going to be making, but there are no good open source auto regressive video models out there today.

insights.claim: Closed products like Grok Imagine extend video by stitching roughly 7-second chunks, while the open approach of feeding the last frame into image-to-video accumulates visible drift — each chunk darker and lower quality until roughly 25 seconds produces a black screen.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: The chunk-stitching trick is the current closed-source moat in long video; drift control, not raw model quality, is the differentiator.

insights.claim: Diffusion attention runs bidirectionally while auto-regression only runs forward, which is why naive frame-sequence video generation goes off the rails, and the winning long-video architecture is likely a hybrid of both.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: A clean architectural test for evaluating claims from video-generation startups about long-form coherence.
insights.quote: The key thing to understand between a auto-aggressive model and a diffusion model is that diffusion attention goes in both directions while auto-aggression it only goes forward in the sequence.

insights.claim: Text diffusion models like Mercury and Diffusion Gemma are mismarketed as faster chat completions when their real differentiation is a different API surface — classifier-free-guidance-style prompts that diffuse a poem, plot structure or storyboard into place with global coherence.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Suggests text-diffusion companies competing on speed will lose; the category needs a product repositioning to find a market.

insights.claim: Inference speed now bottlenecks RL training because slow rollouts on an unsupported or older inference engine force waiting rather than training on off-policy data, so inference optimizations directly accelerate training pipelines.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Inference engine support for a new architecture is now a training-throughput dependency, expanding the addressable market for inference tooling into training labs.

insights.claim: When post-training quantization to NVFP4 degrades a model too far, labs run quantization-aware training or Nvidia-style quantization-over-distillation where the FP4 and full-precision versions are distilled against each other's logits.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Explains why inference engineers now need training skills and why serving quality increasingly depends on training-side investment.

insights.claim: Baseten expects leading agent builders to have continuous-improvement loops in production within a few months to a couple of years, where product traces continuously post-train the model, get A/B tested, and feed back into a better product.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: A concrete timeline for when proprietary traffic data becomes a compounding moat for agent companies rather than a static asset.

insights.claim: GLM 5.2 wrote GPU kernels running in Baseten's own production inference engine, driving a closed loop of forward pass, profile trace, bottleneck identification, kernel rewrite, re-profile and image upload from within a Claude Code harness.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: A working existence proof of models optimizing their own inference — the earliest credible signal of recursive self-improvement in production infrastructure.
insights.quote: Some of the GPU kernels that we run on JLM52 within our inference engine is written by JLM52.

insights.claim: Writing a serving config for an arbitrary new Hugging Face model used to be a core job function and is now one-shottable by a model reading the SGLang docs.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of automation eating a specialized ML-infra job within two years — relevant to headcount assumptions at inference companies.
insights.quote: One big part of my job a couple years ago was for any arbitrary model that came out on Hugging Face, writing a config for it and kind of getting it up and running. And now that get it up and running configs is one-shottable.

insights.claim: Continual learning via weight editing fails because a fact patched into an MLP is only recallable one-shot and does not propagate into second-derivative reasoning, whereas KV cache compaction preserves it usably.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Bets against the weight-update path for continual learning and toward near-infinite compacted KV, which means inference architecture barely changes.

insights.claim: The single biggest inference unlock would be dramatically faster NICs, since KV cache currently makes a two-stage hop through node memory before reaching GPU tensor cores while HBM runs at roughly 4.5 terabits per second.
insights.speaker: Ali Taha
insights.so_what: Points a networking-hardware thesis at the true bottleneck for disaggregated serving — a potential two-orders-of-magnitude prize.
insights.quote: This would give you like almost 100 x speed up when you're doing this aggregated serving between nodes and nodes.

insights.claim: AI usage remains far below mature consumer and business technologies, so the industry should expect multiple further 10x steps in demand, keeping long-tail reliability and token supply as the dominant operational problems.
insights.speaker: Philip Kiely
insights.so_what: The operator-level demand view supports continued capex intensity rather than an inference overbuild.
